# Levels of Reproducibility {#sec-levels}

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Reproducibility has the potential to serve as a minimum
standard for judging scientific claims when full
independent replication of a study is not possible.*

[Roger D. Peng]{.smallcaps}, *Reproducible Research in
Computational Science* (2011)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

By the end of this chapter you will be able to look at
any repository, your own or someone else's, and say
exactly which of four rungs it has reached. You will
also be able to say what still stands between
it and the next one, rather than reach for the
unfalsifiable claim 'fully reproducible.'



::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 40 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** Chapter 1 (the introduction), for the
first, informal pass at the determinant stack this
chapter makes precise; no other chapter is assumed.
Statistically, nothing beyond reading a regression
output, a hazard ratio or an odds ratio with its
confidence interval, is required. No R fluency beyond
reading a short script is assumed; the chapter's own
code chunks are simple enough to follow without having
written R before.

**By the end of this chapter you will be able to
answer:**

- Can you enumerate the layers of the determinant stack
  on which a computational result stands, and say which
  layers common practice pins and which it leaves to
  chance?
- Can you place an analysis on the four-rung ladder of
  this book (L0 locatable, L1 pinned packages, L2 pinned
  environment, L3 verified) and name the artifact that
  marks each transition?
- Can you distinguish capturing reproducibility from
  validating it, and explain why continuous integration
  adds no new pinned layer?
- Can you distinguish a result that is reproduced from
  one that is replicated, and navigate the shifting use
  of those two words across the literature?
- Can you state plainly the level an analysis has
  reached, and no higher, including the candid
  admission that no present framework pins the whole
  stack?

**Outline.**

- Orientation: a result that silently changed on a
  second machine.
- The analyst's contribution: the three judgments no
  tool automates.
- The stack a result stands on: the nine layers, and
  which rungs secure which.
- The ladder: capture sets the level, validation
  confirms it.
- Reproduced, replicated, and a warning about the words.
- Two numbering schemes, and which this book uses.
- The ladder grades every archetype.
- No framework pins the whole stack.
- Worked example: one analysis walked up all four rungs.
- The cohort, continued: placing this book's own
  compendium on the ladder, today.
:::

## Orientation

Consider a registry study of thirty-day
readmission after heart failure. The analyst fits a
mixed-effects model, draws a forest plot, and reports an
adjusted odds ratio of 1.24. The script runs, the
manuscript renders, the paper is accepted. Two years
later a reader requests the code, downloads it, and runs
it on a fresh laptop. The model fits, but differently. A
package that the analysis relied upon has changed its
default optimizer, and the estimate now returned is 1.19.
Which number is the finding? The discrepancy is
computational in origin. The model specified was the same
on both machines; what differed was everything underneath
it, and the analyst never recorded it. Its size, however,
is a statistical finding. An estimate that moves from 1.24
to 1.19 when only the optimizer changes signals a flat or
ill-conditioned likelihood, or a fit that has not
converged. It should be checked, for example by refitting
under several optimizers with `lme4::allFit()`, and
reported as optimizer-sensitive.

This chapter is about naming that 'everything
underneath', and about grading how much of it a given
analysis has secured. We introduced in @sec-intro the
observation that a computational result depends on a
stack of determinants beneath the code and the data,
and that a published script pins almost none of them.
Here we make that observation precise. After setting out
the judgments that remain with the analyst, we shall lay
out the stack layer by layer. We then define the ladder
that this book uses to say how far down the stack a
particular effort has reached: L0 locatable, L1 pinned
packages, L2 pinned environment, and L3 verified. With
the ladder in hand, we consider how the words
'reproduced' and 'replicated' have shifted across the
literature, and how the framework's own numbering differs
from ours. Lastly, we examine how the ladder grades each
archetype, admit that no framework pins the whole stack,
walk one analysis up all four rungs, and then place this
book's own compendium on the ladder.

The ladder is the conceptual backbone of everything
that follows. Every later chapter is, in effect, an
account of how to climb one rung of it. Pinning
packages with a lockfile (@sec-dependencies) is the
L0-to-L1 step. Pinning the environment with a container
(@sec-containers) is the L1-to-L2 step. And verifying
the outputs (@sec-verification) is the L2-to-L3 step.
Before we can teach the climbing we need the ladder
itself, together with the discipline of naming, without
flinching, the rung one has actually reached.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what changed, and what did not

In the registry-study story above, the code and the data
were unchanged between the two runs. What changed, why
does calling the discrepancy purely 'statistical'
mischaracterize its origin, and what statistical question
does it nonetheless raise?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A package the analysis depended on changed its default
optimizer between the two runs. That change sits on the
package-versions layer of the determinant stack, not on
the analysis code or the data. The model specified was
identical on both machines; what differed was an unpinned
determinant beneath it. Calling the discrepancy purely
'statistical' hides a computational failure behind a word
that belongs to a different kind of disagreement, one
about the data or the model. Its size is still a
statistical question. An estimate that moves when only the
optimizer changes comes from a poorly conditioned or
unconverged fit, so it should be refit under other
optimizers and reported as optimizer-sensitive. Pinning
the package makes that fragile estimate reproducible; it
does not make it trustworthy.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

We begin with three judgments at the center of this
chapter that belong to the analyst and are automated by
no tool. The machinery of later chapters exists to
support them.

1. **Choosing, and declaring, the honest level.** A
   framework can compute which rung a repository has
   reached and print it; it cannot decide what the
   author will claim. The judgment that a paper's
   reproducibility statement will match the level
   actually secured, and never assert above it, is the
   analyst's alone. It is the single habit this book
   most wishes to instill.

2. **Matching the investment to the stakes.** Climbing
   the ladder costs effort, and not every analysis
   warrants the climb. A two-day exploratory
   calculation may honestly rest at L0; a registry study
   destined for a guideline warrants L2 or L3. Deciding
   where on the ladder a given project should sit, given
   its lifespan, its audience, and the cost of being
   wrong, is a design decision.

3. **Naming what remains exposed.** No rung of the
   ladder pins the whole stack. The analyst who reaches
   L2 must still ask whether the layers left unpinned
   (the numerical libraries, the random-number
   discipline, the integrity of an external data source)
   matter for this particular analysis. Those that do
   must be closed by hand. Telling a live exposure from
   an inert one is a matter of subject-matter judgment.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: whose judgment is it?

A vendor's reproducibility dashboard reports that a
project has reached 'L2'. Which of the three judgments
above, if any, has the dashboard made for the analyst,
and which remain the analyst's alone?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The dashboard can detect the capture artifacts (a
lockfile and a container recipe) and so can compute the
rung mechanically; that much is automatable. It cannot
decide whether L2 was the right level to target for this
analysis given its stakes. Nor can it know which
unpinned layers, among the numerical libraries, the RNG
kind, or an external data source, are live exposures for
this particular question. Judging
the match of effort to stakes, and naming what remains
exposed, stay with the analyst no matter how good the
dashboard is.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

New terms are defined again on first use; they are
collected here for reference.

- **Determinant stack.** The layered set of things a
  computational result depends upon, from the hardware
  at the base through the environment and the packages
  to the analysis code and the data at the top. A layer
  is 'pinned' when it has been fixed to a recorded
  value.
- **Capture.** Fixing an input so that it cannot drift:
  writing a lockfile, building a container image.
  Capture sets the reproducibility level.
- **Validation.** Confirming that the captured inputs
  actually suffice, by rebuilding and re-running.
  Validation does not pin anything new; it checks.
- **The level ladder (L0 to L3).** The four-rung scale,
  L0 locatable, L1 pinned packages, L2 pinned
  environment, L3 verified, used throughout this book to
  grade how far down the stack an analysis has been
  secured.
- **Reproduced.** Obtaining the same computational
  result by re-executing the same code on the same data.
  Contrast **replicated**, obtaining a consistent
  finding from a new study with new data.
- **Lockfile.** A file, such as `renv.lock`, recording
  the exact version of every package an analysis used.
- **Container image.** A packaged environment, built
  from a recipe, that carries the operating system, the
  system libraries, and the language runtime, and
  provides the same environment wherever a container
  runtime for its platform runs.
- **RNG kind.** The random-number algorithm in force,
  set by `RNGkind()`. Two runs with the same seed but a
  different kind draw different numbers.
:::

## The stack a result stands on

We turn now to the determinants, because the ladder is
only intelligible once we see what it grades. A
computational result is the output of running some code
against some data. However, the code and the data are
only the two topmost of a tall stack of dependencies.
The result is a function of the whole stack, not of its
top two layers alone. Arranging the determinants from the
hardware upward to the analysis logic yields the nine
layers this book uses; a finer split, such as one that
separates the document toolchain, yields ten or more.

At the base sits the **hardware**: the processor
architecture, its instruction-set extensions, and the
behavior of its floating-point unit. Above it lie the
**numerical libraries**, the BLAS and LAPACK
implementations that perform the linear algebra beneath
every regression and every matrix decomposition. These
matter more than their obscurity suggests. A different
BLAS, or the same BLAS run with a different thread
count, reorders the floating-point summations and can
change a result in its low-order digits. Above these
sit the **operating system and its system libraries**:
the kernel, the C library, the locale data, the fonts,
and the document toolchain of `pandoc` and LaTeX. Then
comes the **R runtime** itself, whose default behaviors
shift between releases. The random-number change of
R 3.6.0 and the `stringsAsFactors` change of R 4.0.0
both illustrate the point.

Above the runtime sit the layers most analysts think of
first. The **package versions**, the exact release of
every R package the analysis loads, are the layer that
churns fastest and breaks analyses most often. The
**session configuration** is a cluster of settings that
shape the session before any user code runs. It
comprises the random-number kind set by `RNGkind()`, the
contrasts used for factor variables, and the number of
printed `digits`. It also comprises the locale that
governs sorting, and the time zone that governs date
arithmetic. Then come the two layers the
analyst actually writes. These are the **analysis
code**, including every `set.seed()` call and the order
of execution, and the **input data**, its content and its
integrity. Finally, threaded through the whole stack,
sits **intrinsic non-determinism**: the use of the
wall-clock, race conditions in parallel code, and
iteration over unordered structures are each capable of
producing a different answer on two runs of identical
inputs.

Common practice pins very few of these layers. A bare
published script pins exactly one layer with any
reliability, the analysis code, since the code is the
file itself. If the reader is fortunate, it pins a
second, the data, when it has been deposited alongside.
Every other layer is left to whatever the next machine
happens to provide. @fig-determinant-stack maps the stack
against the rung of the ladder that first secures each
layer. Three layers (the hardware, the numerical
libraries, and intrinsic non-determinism) are secured by
no rung of the capture ladder at all. The numerical
libraries are the case most often misread. A container
image determines which BLAS is installed, but the ladder
does not require that library to be fixed, and the thread
count and the processor still vary between machines. No
rung therefore guarantees this layer.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_determinant_stack(
  captures = determinant_layers()$layer,
  title = 'Which rung first secures each layer')
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

Package versions are secured at L1, the operating system and R runtime at L2, and the analysis code and data are merely locatable at L0. Three further layers, the hardware, the numerical libraries, and intrinsic non-determinism, are pinned by no rung of the capture ladder. Two settings of the session-configuration layer deserve
a word, because they are the settings most often
forgotten by an analyst who has already adopted a
lockfile and a container. The random-number kind is the
more dangerous. An analysis that seeds its generator and
draws a sample is reproducible only if the algorithm
behind the seed is also fixed. The change of the default
`sample.kind` in R 3.6.0 broke exactly this, silently,
for every analysis that had set a seed under the old
default: the same seed now drew different samples, so no
seeded result regenerated digit for digit. Whether a
result also changed as a statistical matter is a separate
question. @sec-testing answers it on the book's cohort
(@tbl-baseline-rng): the shift is a fraction of one Monte
Carlo standard error, so the bound reproduces
statistically although not seed-exactly. Given that
simulation studies, multiple imputation, and bootstrap
confidence intervals are staples
of health research, the RNG kind is a first-order concern.
The locale is the second. `sort()` and `order()` on a
character vector depend on `LC_COLLATE`, so an analysis
developed under one locale and re-run under another can
reorder a table without any error. The decimal mark is a
different matter. R keeps `LC_NUMERIC` at 'C' and warns if
code changes it, so base parsing reads '.' as the decimal
mark whatever the system locale. A file written with
decimal commas is read as text unless the reading function
is told otherwise, for example with `dec = ','` in
`read.csv()`.

The RNG kind also shows why a setting can belong to two
layers at once. The R release sets the *default* kind, so
the default is part of the R runtime and is fixed at L2.
Code or a project `.Rprofile` can *override* the default,
and an override is session configuration, fixed only by an
explicit `RNGkind()` call in the analysis code. The same
distinction between a default and an override recurs
across the stack, and the table below states it for the
settings this book returns to most often.

| Setting | What fixes the default | What can override it | What closes the override |
|----------------------------|--------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| RNG kind (`sample.kind`) | The R release (R runtime, L2) | Code, `.Rprofile`, a package | An explicit `RNGkind()` call in the analysis |
| `stringsAsFactors` | The R release (R runtime, L2) | The argument in each call | Writing the argument in the code |
| Locale and time zone | The image or the host (L2 when the image sets them) | `Sys.setlocale()`, `Sys.setenv(TZ = )` | Setting them in the image or in the analysis |
| BLAS and LAPACK | The image or the host (no rung) | The library path, the thread count | No rung; fixing the thread count narrows it, and a stated tolerance absorbs what remains |

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: locating a failure on the stack

An epidemiologist reports that a colleague, re-running
her cohort analysis, obtained a least-squares regression
coefficient identical to five decimal places but a
different value in the sixth. The fit was computed as
`solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y))` on a large design
matrix. The code, the data, the package versions, and the
operating system were all identical. Which layer of the
determinant stack is the most likely culprit, and is the
discrepancy a bug?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Neither the code nor the data nor the pinned layers can
be at fault, since all were identical. A discrepancy
confined to the low-order digits is the signature of the
numerical-library layer. `crossprod()` hands the matrix
product to the BLAS, and `solve()` hands the linear
system to LAPACK. The two machines used a different BLAS
implementation, or the same one with a different thread
count, and so the floating-point summations were
reordered. It is not a bug in the
analysis. It is the reason that byte-for-byte identity
across different hardware is a stronger claim than
number-for-number agreement on a fixed architecture.
And it is a layer that no rung of the capture ladder
pins.
:::
:::

## The ladder: capture sets the level, validation confirms it

With the stack in view we can define the ladder. The
central design idea, which we take from the framework
this book uses and develop as a general principle, is
that the features acting on reproducibility divide into
two kinds that are constantly confused. Separating them
is what makes an honest grade possible.

The **capture axes** fix inputs, and therefore set the
level. There are two of them: the package backend, which
pins the package layer, and the computational
environment, which pins the operating system, the
runtime, and the system libraries. Adding a capture
feature raises the level; removing one lowers it. The
**validation layer** confirms the captured level without
capturing anything new. Its members are continuous
integration, the dependency-consistency check, and the
output-verification command. Removing a validation
feature leaves a repository exactly as reconstructable as
before; it only stops the automated checking. This is why
continuous integration, which we develop in
@sec-verification, is best understood as the harness that
runs the verification rather than as a layer of
reproducibility in its own right. Pinning is capture;
re-running to confirm is validation.

The four rungs follow from this distinction. Levels L0
through L2 are reached by the capture axes, and L3 is
reached by the validation layer. @tbl-ladder states each
rung, what it pins, the artifact that marks it, and what
the rung means for a reader of health research.


::: {#tbl-ladder .cell tbl-cap='The reproducibility ladder used throughout this book. Each rung names what it pins, the primary artifact that marks it, and what reaching it means for a reader of health research.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tibble)
library(knitr)

ladder <- tibble::tibble(
  Level = c('L0 locatable',
            'L1 pinned packages',
            'L2 pinned environment',
            'L3 verified'),
  `What is pinned` = c(
    'Nothing computational; the source is under version control',
    'The exact version of every R package',
    'The operating system, the R runtime, and the system libraries as well',
    'Nothing new; the recorded outputs are shown to regenerate within a stated tolerance from a clean rebuild'),
  `Primary artifact` = c(
    'A version-controlled repository',
    'A lockfile such as renv.lock',
    'A container image or a Nix environment',
    'A passing baseline test, run after a clean rebuild, that compares regenerated outputs with values recorded in a committed baseline file within a stated tolerance'),
  `Health-research reading` = c(
    'A reviewer can find the code but cannot yet rebuild it',
    'A colleague installs the same packages the analysis used',
    'The analysis yields the same numbers on a different machine',
    'The reported table has been shown to regenerate, not merely asserted to'))

knitr::kable(ladder)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Level                 |What is pinned                                                                                           |Primary artifact                                                                                                                                                  |Health-research reading                                                 |
|:---------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
|L0 locatable          |Nothing computational; the source is under version control                                               |A version-controlled repository                                                                                                                                   |A reviewer can find the code but cannot yet rebuild it                  |
|L1 pinned packages    |The exact version of every R package                                                                     |A lockfile such as renv.lock                                                                                                                                      |A colleague installs the same packages the analysis used                |
|L2 pinned environment |The operating system, the R runtime, and the system libraries as well                                    |A container image or a Nix environment                                                                                                                            |The analysis yields the same numbers on a different machine             |
|L3 verified           |Nothing new; the recorded outputs are shown to regenerate within a stated tolerance from a clean rebuild |A passing baseline test, run after a clean rebuild, that compares regenerated outputs with values recorded in a committed baseline file within a stated tolerance |The reported table has been shown to regenerate, not merely asserted to |


:::
:::


L3 is the one rung that cannot be read off a file
listing. An analysis is at **L3, verified**, when its
recorded outputs have been shown to regenerate within a
stated tolerance from a clean rebuild. The showing is done
by a *baseline test*, that is, a test that recomputes the
reported quantities and compares them with values
recorded in a committed baseline file. The comparison is
made within a tolerance written into the test. A clean
rebuild whose tests pass, but which compares nothing
against a recorded baseline, demonstrates that the
environment builds and the code runs. That is L2
confirmed, not L3. But why a tolerance, and not exact
equality? Estimates are floating-point numbers, and exact
equality would fail on harmless differences in the last
digits while saying nothing about whether the substantive
result moved. In the framework this book uses,
`zzc verify --full` applies exactly this definition. It
records L3 only when the image rebuilds, the test suite
passes, and at least one baseline test (a file named
`inst/tinytest/test-baseline*.R`) exists and ran.
Otherwise it reports the project as rebuilt and tested,
L2, with no baseline comparison. Continuous integration
that re-runs the check on every change keeps an L3 claim
current. However, it is the baseline comparison, not the
automation, that earns the rung.

The rungs are cumulative. An L2 analysis is also
locatable and package-pinned; the label names the
highest rung reached. The transition that matters most
for a first-year student to internalize is the one
between L1 and L2. A lockfile alone, the L1 artifact,
pins the packages but not the R version, the operating
system, or the system libraries a package links against.
A lockfile restored under a different R version may fail
to install or, more insidiously, may install and behave
differently. The container image, the L2 artifact, fixes
what the lockfile cannot. The two are complements, not
substitutes, and a genuinely pinned-environment analysis
carries both.

The ladder consolidates several graded views of
reproducibility that the literature has offered in
different vocabularies. @peng2011 arranged computational
work along a spectrum, from the merely published, through
code available, code and data available, and linked and
executable, to full replication. Our L0, L1, and L2 track
the lower and middle reaches of that spectrum. The
artifact-review badges used by the ACM
and several computing venues express a related ordering,
from artifacts that are available, through artifacts
evaluated as functional and then reusable, to results
independently reproduced [@acm2020]. The badges and the
rungs grade different things and should not be equated.
The 'functional' and 'reusable' badges grade how well an
artifact is documented and exercised. They do not grade
the package-versus-environment pinning depth that
separates L1 from L2. Likewise, reaching L3 is not the
same act as earning a venue's reproduction badge, which is
awarded by reviewers under that venue's own policy. The
reader who needs a badge should read the venue's current
definition directly. The L-scheme adds no new definition
of reproducibility. It maps these graded
views onto artifacts a tool can detect, so that the level
of a repository can be determined mechanically and
reported honestly, rather than asserted by its author.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: capture or validation?

A laboratory adds a continuous-integration workflow that
rebuilds its compendium and runs the tests on every push.
A colleague objects that this cannot improve
reproducibility, because it pins no new layer of the
determinant stack. Is the colleague correct, and has the
laboratory wasted its effort?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The colleague is correct on the narrow point and wrong on
the conclusion. Continuous integration is a validation
feature, not a capture feature: it pins no new layer, and
removing it would leave the compendium exactly as
reconstructable as before. What it adds is confirmation.
It re-runs the captured analysis in a clean environment
that carries none of the author's undeclared state. It
therefore catches the silent decay that a
captured-but-never-retested analysis suffers, and the
'works on my machine' failure at its source. The
laboratory has moved from L2 asserted to L2 confirmed: the
environment is shown to build and the code to run. A
baseline test, comparing regenerated outputs with recorded
values, is what would make it L3.
:::
:::

## Reproduced, replicated, and a warning about the words

The ladder grades re-execution, and re-execution is only
one of the things the word 'reproducibility' is made to
carry. We need to fix the terms before reading the
literature, because the same two words are attached to
opposite meanings across the sources a reader will meet.

The National Academies, in their 2019 consensus report,
adopt the distinction this book follows [@nas2019].
*Reproducibility* is obtaining consistent computational
results using the same input data, the same code, and the
same conditions of analysis. That is, it is a statement
about re-execution, and it is what the ladder grades.
*Replicability* is obtaining consistent results across
studies aimed at the same question, each with its own
data. It is a statement about whether a scientific
finding holds on new data. The two are independent. A
result can be perfectly reproducible and entirely wrong,
if the code faithfully regenerates a mistaken number
every time. Conversely, a finding can replicate across
laboratories while no single analysis in the set is
computationally reproducible. Leek and Peng press exactly
this point, that a reproducible analysis can still be
wrong, and that reproducibility is therefore a floor and
not a ceiling [@leek2015]. Patil, Peng, and Leek go
further and offer a statistical framing of the
distinction. They cast replication as a question about the
agreement of estimates across studies rather than about
the re-running of code [@patil2016].

How do other vocabularies relate to this one? The current
ACM artifact-badge vocabulary, in its 2020 revision,
aligns its direction of use with the National Academies
convention rather than inverting it [@acm2020]. However,
the two draw the boundary differently. Under the National
Academies convention, 'Reproduced' means obtaining a
prior result using the same code and data; the same team
re-running their own analysis qualifies. Under the ACM
'Results Reproduced' badge, the re-running must be done by
a team other than the original authors, using the
author's provided artifacts. Both conventions therefore
point 'Reproduced' toward re-execution with the original
artifacts and 'Replicated' toward independence. The ACM
badge, however, specifically requires a different team,
while the National Academies definition does not.

The genuine word-swap that trips students belongs to two
other places. One is the pre-2020 ACM badging, which
attached the two words in the opposite direction along
the re-execution axis. The other is a set of biomedical
and other field-specific usages, which a reader may still
encounter, where 'reproduce' names an independent study
rather than a re-run. A reader who carries the sense of
the words from one of those older documents
into a current one will be misled. The misreading happens
silently and without any error to warn them, in exactly
the manner of a shifted package default. This book
therefore fixes the meaning and states it once.
Throughout, 'reproduced' carries the National Academies
sense. L3 means that the captured analysis, rebuilt from
its pinned definition and re-run, regenerates its own
recorded outputs within a stated tolerance, as checked by
a baseline test. It is deliberately not replication in
the sense of an independent study on new data, which no
software framework can supply. When the reader meets
'reproduced' or 'replicated' in a journal's author
instructions or a venue's badging policy, the first task
is to determine which convention that document uses.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Another warning about the words: 'validation'

This chapter uses 'validation' and the L3 label
'verified' for a narrow act: confirming that a previously
captured value still holds, as a baseline test does.
Regulated industry work, pharmaceutical and other
FDA-adjacent settings among them, attaches 'validation' to
something larger: a formal, documented process confirming
that a system is fit for its intended use, as under 21 CFR
11.10(a) [@cfr21part11]. European regulators expect
something comparable of a sponsor's analysis tools. A
graduate moving into that kind of work will meet the
regulated sense on arrival; this book's narrower one does
not prepare them for the paperwork that comes with it.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: which word, which sense?

A manuscript's cover letter states that the authors
'reproduced the primary finding in an independent
cohort.' Under the National Academies convention this
chapter follows, is that reproduction or replication, and
why does the sentence as written risk being misread?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

It is replication: an independent cohort means new data,
and the National Academies convention attaches
'replicated' to a new study and 'reproduced' to re-running
the original artifacts on the original data. The sentence
risks being misread because of the current ACM badge
sense. A reader applying it would expect the word
'reproduced' to mean an independent team re-ran the
authors' own artifacts, not that a second cohort was
collected. The fix is to write 'replicated', not
'reproduced', or to spell out which convention is meant.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter defines the ladder rather than climbing it.
Its one executed placement, the cohort compendium in
'The cohort, continued' below, is computed from the
repository's artifacts each time the chapter renders,
not asserted here. Every rung above the one that section
prints is left to the chapters this ladder points toward.
:::

## Two numbering schemes, and which this book uses

Before applying the ladder to particular archetypes, we
need to dispose of a source of confusion. A reader who
consults the documentation of the framework this book uses
will encounter a second numbering scheme, and the two are
easily confused.

The framework's teaching materials include a vignette that
presents a *five-level* ramp. Level 1 is a basic R project
with manual package management, and Level 2 is the
addition of `renv`. Level 3 is the addition of Docker,
Level 4 the addition of unit testing, and Level 5 the
addition of continuous integration. That scale counts *which tools a
project has adopted*, and it is a pedagogical on-ramp,
meant to be walked from the bottom as a project matures.
It is a useful thing, but it is not the scale of this book.

The scale of this book is the *architectural* ladder of
the preceding sections, L0 through L3. It grades something
different: *how far down the determinant stack a result has
been locked, and whether the lock has been verified*. The
two axes are related but not identical. Adopting `renv`
(the tool scheme's Level 2) is what lifts a project to L1.
Adopting a container (the tool scheme's Level 3) is what
lifts it to L2. The tool scheme's testing and
continuous-integration levels belong to the validation
layer that reaches L3. However, one can imagine a project
that has adopted every tool and still verified nothing.
The architectural ladder, not the tool count, is what
tells the reader whether the result has been shown to
reproduce.

To avoid ambiguity we adopt a single convention. This book
uses the L0 to L3 architectural ladder throughout, in every
chapter and every worked example. Where the framework's own
documentation speaks of 'Level 1' through 'Level 5', it is
using the tool-adoption ramp, and the reader should read it
as such and not conflate it with our L0 to L3. When we
write a bare 'L2', we always mean the architectural rung.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: two scales, one word

A student writes in a lab notebook, 'the project is at
Level 2, so it is container-pinned.' Using this chapter's
two scales, is the inference safe?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. On the tool-adoption ramp, Level 2 means `renv` has
been added, which is the architectural chapter's L1, not
its L2; the container arrives at the ramp's Level 3. The
student's sentence silently mixed the two scales' numbers.
The safe habit is to never write a bare number without
saying which scale it belongs to. This book's own
convention, stated above, is to let an unqualified 'L2'
always mean the architectural rung.
:::
:::

## The ladder grades every archetype

Does the ladder apply equally to every kind of
compendium? @tbl-archetype-weight in @sec-compendium shows
how each archetype reads it. A data-analysis project and a
manuscript read it the same way. An R package reaches L2
by `R CMD check` and L3 by a baseline on its function
outputs, and a blog applies the ladder post by post. The
case most easily missed is the simulation study. Its
exposure on the session-configuration layer is acute,
because its outputs are functions of the random-number
stream. An unseeded or wrongly seeded simulation can
therefore sit at L2, with a perfectly pinned environment,
and still fail to reproduce. For this archetype the
discipline of fixing the RNG kind and the seed is the
difference between a nominal L2 and a real one. The ladder
is a property of the determinant stack, which every
archetype shares, and not of any particular directory
layout.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: grading an R package

An R package has `renv.lock`, a Dockerfile, and a full
`testthat`-style test suite that passes in a clean
rebuild, but none of its tests compare a function's
output with a value recorded earlier. What rung has it
reached, and what is missing for the next one?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

It is at L2, pinned environment, confirmed: the lockfile
and the container pin the packages and the environment,
and the clean rebuild and passing test suite show the
package builds and runs. It is not at L3, because none of
its tests is a baseline test. Passing means the code ran
without error, not that a key function's output still
matches a recorded reference value within a tolerance.
Reaching L3 needs at least one test that compares a fixed
input's output against a value committed earlier.
:::
:::

## No framework pins the whole stack

Reaching L2 or L3 does not pin the entire determinant
stack, and no present framework pins all of it.

By its own published accounting, which splits the stack
more finely than this chapter into about ten
determinants, the framework this book uses robustly pins
about four. These are the operating system and system
libraries (as strongly as its base image is pinned), the
R package versions (nominally, through the lockfile), the
locale and time zone, and the source code. It leaves
others to convention or to the base image. The
random-number kind is not pinned by default. The BLAS and
LAPACK implementation is inherited from the base image
(the generated Dockerfile sets `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`, which
fixes the thread count but not the library). The
integrity of external data is recorded by provenance but
not by checksum, and the fonts and the graphics device
are pinned only for some profiles. We know of no
integrative framework that currently pins these layers,
and an honest L2 or L3 claim names them. The reader will
therefore find, at each rung of the ladder in the
chapters ahead, an explicit account of what is secured
and what remains exposed. That account includes the framework this book teaches.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: naming the gap honestly

A compendium reaches L3 by this chapter's definition: it
rebuilds from clean, its tests pass, and a baseline test
compares a reported hazard ratio with a recorded value
within a stated tolerance. Is it now safe to call the
analysis fully reproducible, with nothing left to
disclose?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. L3 shows that the pinned definition regenerates the
reported quantity within a stated tolerance. It does not
pin the numerical libraries, the hardware, or intrinsic
non-determinism, none of which any rung of the capture
ladder secures. An honest statement at L3 still names
these as exposed, for example that the bootstrap interval
has not been checked for agreement across a different
BLAS or CPU architecture. 'Fully reproducible' claims a
closed stack that no present framework, including the one
this book teaches, actually closes.
:::
:::

## Worked example

To make the ladder concrete, consider a single analysis
walked up all four rungs. A biostatistician has a folder
containing `analysis.R`, which reads `cohort.csv`, fits a
Cox model with the `survival` package, and writes a hazard
ratio to `results.csv`. We shall place it on the ladder and
name each transition.

At the start the folder is on the analyst's laptop and
nowhere else. It is at no rung of the ladder at all, because
it cannot even be found by a second person. The first act,
placing the folder under version control and pushing it to
a repository, lifts it to **L0, locatable**. A reviewer can
now find `analysis.R` and read it. Nothing computational is
pinned; a reviewer who runs it will install whatever version
of `survival` happens to be current, which may not be the
version the analyst used.

The analyst now runs `renv::init()` and `renv::snapshot()`,
which we develop in @sec-dependencies. This writes a
`renv.lock` recording that the analysis used `survival`
version 3.5-7, together with the exact version of every
other package in the closure. The folder is now at **L1,
pinned packages**. A colleague who restores from the
lockfile obtains the same `survival` the analyst used. But
the colleague's laptop runs a newer R and a different
operating system, and one of the packages links against a
system library that is absent, so the restore fails to
build.

To close that gap the analyst adds a container, developed in
@sec-containers, built from a dated `rocker` base image
pinned by its content digest. The image carries a fixed
operating system, a fixed R, and the system libraries the
packages need, and the lockfile restores inside it. The
folder is now at **L2, pinned environment**. It will build
the same environment on the colleague's laptop, on a
reviewer's, and on a server. Because the analyst computes
bootstrap confidence intervals for the hazard ratio, the
analyst also sets the RNG kind with an explicit
`RNGkind()` call in `analysis.R`, and passes a seed at the
call that draws the resamples. Neither goes in the project
`.Rprofile`. A seed set at session start makes every draw
depend on whatever consumed random numbers earlier in the
session, the rule @sec-testing develops. This closes a
session-configuration exposure that L2 does not close by
default.

Finally the analyst adds a verification step, developed in
@sec-verification. The step rebuilds the image from clean
and re-runs `analysis.R`. It then runs a baseline test
comparing the regenerated hazard ratio and its confidence
limits with the values recorded in a committed baseline
file, within a stated relative tolerance. It passes, and
a continuous-integration service re-runs it on every
change. The folder is now at **L3, verified**. That is,
the reported hazard ratio has been shown to regenerate,
not merely asserted to. The honest reproducibility
statement for the paper can now name the rung, the
artifacts, and the layers that remain outside the
guarantee. No rung pins the hardware, the numerical
libraries, or intrinsic non-determinism. For this
analysis they amount chiefly to the cross-architecture
numerical determinism of the bootstrap.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: which rung, which artifact

The biostatistician's colleague restores the lockfile but
skips the container, then reports the analysis as
'reproducible.' Which rung has the colleague actually
reached, and what single artifact would the colleague need
to add to reach the next one?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Restoring the lockfile reaches L1, pinned packages, and no
further. The operating system, the R runtime, and the
system libraries the colleague's machine happens to carry
are still whatever that machine provides, not what the
original analyst used. Calling this 'reproducible' without
qualification overstates by at least one rung. The single
artifact that closes the gap to L2 is the container image,
built from the same recipe the original analyst used, which
pins the layers the lockfile cannot reach.
:::
:::

The worked example above follows a composite
biostatistician. We now perform the same placement
exercise on this book's own running cohort compendium, as
it stands in this repository when the chapter is rendered.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

cohort <- clean_cohort(raw)
nrow(raw)
#> [1] 338
nrow(cohort)
#> [1] 337
```
:::


The extract loads and cleans without error, and
`clean_cohort()` drops the one duplicated `mrn` the
Conventions page describes, leaving the row count shown
above. Whether the compendium is locatable, and whether
anything beneath the code is pinned, is a question about
which artifacts the repository holds, so we check rather
than assert it.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

  source_code = file.exists('../../R/cohort.R'),
  data_generator = file.exists('../scripts/simulate_cohort.R'),
  lockfile = file.exists('../../renv.lock'),
  dockerfile = file.exists('../../Dockerfile')
)
repo_state
#>    source_code data_generator       lockfile     dockerfile 
#>           TRUE           TRUE           TRUE          FALSE
rung <- if (repo_state[['lockfile']] && repo_state[['dockerfile']]) {
  'L2'
} else if (repo_state[['lockfile']]) {
  'L1'
} else {
  'L0'
}
rung_name <- c(
  L0 = 'locatable', L1 = 'pinned packages',
  L2 = 'pinned environment'
)[[rung]]
next_artifact <- c(
  L0 = 'a lockfile, `renv.lock`',
  L1 = 'a container recipe, a `Dockerfile`',
  L2 = 'a baseline test that passes after a clean rebuild'
)[[rung]]
```
:::


The code is under version control, so a reader of this
book can find `R/cohort.R` and read exactly what ran. The
extract itself is not committed; the repository holds the
generator, `analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R`, which
writes the synthetic extract from a fixed seed. That much
is L0, locatable. The lockfile entry above is
TRUE and the Dockerfile entry is
FALSE, so on its capture
artifacts this compendium is at
**L1, pinned packages**. What it still lacks for the
next rung is a container recipe, a `Dockerfile`. Any layer that no present
artifact pins is left to whatever R, system libraries, and
packages happen to be installed on the machine that runs
this chunk. The chapters on pinning packages
(@sec-dependencies) and pinning the environment
(@sec-containers) teach the artifacts that mark L1 and
L2. The verification chapter (@sec-verification) is the
one that can lift the compendium to L3, once a baseline
test compares a quantity computed from `cohort` against a
value recorded today; the chunk above does not look for

this cell after reading those later chapters is looking at

added, is the rung those lines print.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Collaborating with an LLM

We turn finally to the use of a large language model,
which is a capable assistant for reasoning about levels.
However, it is confident in a register that this chapter
has just taught the reader to distrust, and its
confidence is not calibrated to the honest level.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

One rule comes first (habit 3). Never paste or upload
protected health information, identifiable records, or data
held under a data use agreement, nor outputs derived from
them, into a model or a coding agent unless three conditions
all hold. The institution has approved that endpoint for
that class of data. The IRB protocol and the consent permit
the processing. The data use agreement, or the provider's
terms, permits it. If any of the three is unclear, the
answer is no.

The third condition is the one most often missed.
Institutional approval of a tool does not override the terms
under which a data provider released the data. NIH, for
example, treats sharing controlled-access data with
third-party generative AI tools through prompts as a breach
of the data use certification, and a model trained on such
data as a derivative that may not be distributed without
approval [@nihgenai2025].

Describe the structure instead: the column names and types,
or a small synthetic example generated from the data
dictionary, never edited from real rows. A coding agent sees
whatever files are in its working tree, so run it in a
checkout or container where the real data is not mounted.

An agent also acts, so confine it to a branch and keep merges,
pushes, and deposits for yourself (@sec-llm-delegate).
:::


A directory listing can itself be identifying when file
names carry site or participant codes. List only the code,
configuration, and lock files, and leave data directories
out. The following triples illustrate productive prompts
and the verification each demands.

**Prompt.** 'Here is the listing of my project's code and
configuration files, with the data directories omitted.
What reproducibility level has it reached on the L0 to L3
ladder, and what would it take to reach the next rung?'

*Watch for.* Reading a `renv.lock` as L1 and a
`Dockerfile` as L2 is the right heuristic as far as it
goes. However, no one can tell from a listing whether the
lockfile is current, whether the image is pinned by a
mutable tag or an immutable digest, or whether a
verification run has ever passed. Check whether the answer
reports L3 on the strength of a continuous-integration
file that has never been run green.

*Verification.* Confirm each rung against the artifact
itself, not its filename. For L1, check that the lockfile is
in step with the code. For L2, check that the base image
carries a digest and that the library is not shadowed by a
bind mount. For L3, find an actual passing run of a
baseline test after a clean rebuild, and read the test to
confirm it compares outputs with recorded values under a
stated tolerance. The presence of a file is capture
asserted; a green baseline run is validation observed.

**Prompt.** 'Below are the four rungs of a reproducibility
ladder with their definitions, followed by a description of
my project. Place the project on the ladder. For each rung,
name the artifact in the description that meets its
definition, or say what is missing. The rungs are
cumulative. Say what you could not determine from the
description.'

Supply the rows of @tbl-ladder and the paragraph on
cumulative rungs as the definitions, since a model cannot
apply a scale it has not been given. Describe the project in
prose: what is under version control, whether a lockfile
exists, what the `Dockerfile`'s `FROM` line says, and what
the tests compare.

*Watch for.* Check whether the answer applies the cumulative
rule, or credits L2 to a `Dockerfile` in a project with no
lockfile. Check whether it treats a base image named by tag
as pinned in the same way as one named by digest. Check also
whether it awards L3 to a test suite that compares nothing
with a recorded baseline, which this chapter calls L2
confirmed, not L3.

*Verification.* Place the project yourself, from the
artifacts, before reading the answer, and compare the two
placements rung by rung. Then give the model a case whose
answer you know, such as a project with a `Dockerfile` and
no lockfile, and confirm that it does not award L2. A model
that misplaces the known case should not be trusted on the
unknown one.

**Prompt.** 'My simulation gives slightly different numbers
each time even inside the container. Why, and is it a bug?'

*Watch for.* Check whether the answer blames a layer that
the container has already pinned, such as a package version
or the operating system. Check also that it distinguishes an
unseeded RNG (a real defect) from low-order-digit variation
due to BLAS threading (an inherent limit at L2).

*Verification.* Trace the discrepancy to a layer of the
determinant stack. If the numbers differ in all digits, look
to the RNG kind and the seed, which the analyst controls. If
they differ only in the low-order digits, suspect the
numerical-library layer, which no rung of the capture ladder
pins, and decide whether that residual matters for the
inference at hand.

*A better prompt.* 'My simulation, run twice in the same
container, gives the two outputs pasted below. Also pasted
are the `sessionInfo()` output, which names the BLAS and
LAPACK libraries, the `RNGkind()` output, the line of my code
that sets the seed, and the thread count. Say which layer of
the determinant stack each difference most plausibly comes
from, and for each give one command I can run to confirm or
exclude it.'

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. Two of
these ask you to work with an analysis or a paper of your
own, so they have no single correct answer; for those the
box says what a good answer establishes.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

No single correct answer. What a good answer establishes is
that you can name the layers in order and attach an
artifact, or an admission, to each.

Work up from the base. The **hardware** is pinned by
nothing short of running on the same machine. The
**numerical libraries** are pinned by no rung. The
container image determines which BLAS is installed, but
the ladder does not require it to be fixed, and the thread
count and the processor still vary. The
**operating system and system libraries** are pinned by
the container image. The **R runtime** is likewise pinned
by the container image, and merely *recorded* by the
lockfile's `R` block. The **package versions** are pinned
by `renv.lock`. The **session configuration** is partly
pinned by the image through the locale and the time zone,
and not pinned at all for the RNG kind, the contrasts, and
the printed digits. The **analysis code** is pinned by
version control, while the **input data** are pinned by a
checksum or an archived deposit, and are often only
locatable. Lastly, **intrinsic non-determinism**, such as
parallel reduction order, is pinned by nothing.

Your lowest unpinned layer is most likely either the
numerical libraries or the session configuration, and both
answers are common and honest. If your lowest unpinned
layer is the input data, you have discovered something
more urgent than anything this chapter teaches, because
the analysis is not reconstructable at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

No single correct answer. What a good answer establishes is
that the rung is read off the *deposited artifacts*, not off
the quality of the paper or the reputation of the authors.

The procedure is mechanical. Is there code and data that
can be located? That is L0. Is there a lockfile, or an
equivalent exact version record? That is L1. Is there a
container recipe, or another artifact pinning the runtime
and the system libraries? That is L2. Is there evidence
that the outputs were regenerated from the pinned
definition and compared with recorded values within a
stated tolerance, shown by a baseline test and a CI log or
verification report of it passing? That is L3. A CI log
that only shows the code ran is not enough. Stop at the
highest rung for which an artifact is actually present.

The reproducibility statement should then claim that rung
and no more. For the common L0 case: 'The analysis code and
the derived dataset are deposited at [location]. The
software environment was not recorded, so re-execution may
require package versions that differ from those used here.'
The second clause is the part most papers omit, and it is
the part that makes the statement honest rather than
merely modest.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

Two determinants an image does not pin, with a
circumstance for each.

**The numerical libraries.** An image built on a base
that links against a BLAS chosen at run time, or one run
on hosts that expose different thread counts or
processors, will reorder floating-point summations. Two
runs of the same image on two machines can then return a
least-squares coefficient, computed through `crossprod()`
and `solve()`, agreeing to five decimal places and
differing in the sixth. The image pinned the
software and not the arithmetic beneath it.

**The session configuration, specifically the RNG kind.**
An image fixes the R version, and the R version determines
the *default* sampler, so this exposure is narrower than
it first appears. It bites when the analysis sets
`RNGkind()` itself, or inherits it from a project
`.Rprofile` that is mounted rather than baked in, or when
a package changes the generator as a side effect. Two runs
then draw different samples from the same seed, and a
bootstrap interval moves.

A third acceptable answer is the input data: an image
mounting a host directory reproduces the environment and
not the extract, so a changed file underneath produces a
different result with the image unchanged. A fourth is
intrinsic non-determinism from parallelism, where the
reduction order of a parallel sum varies run to run on the
same machine.

In general, a container pins the environment, and the
environment is not the whole stack.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

'Level 4' on the framework's scale means the project has
adopted a particular set of *tools*: an R project, `renv`,
Docker, and unit testing. It is a statement about tool
adoption, and it is read from the bottom up, so Level 4
implies the first three as well.

What it tells you about the architectural ladder is
therefore quite a lot, but indirectly and with one gap. The
presence of `renv` implies the machinery for L1; the
presence of Docker implies the machinery for L2. What it
does not tell you is whether any of it has been
*verified*, because the tool scale counts adoption and the
architectural ladder grades locking and verification. A
project can hold every tool in the list and have never
rebuilt from its pinned definition. In that case it sits
at L2 and is asserted rather than shown to reproduce. L3
requires a baseline comparison, which neither Level 4 nor
Level 5 implies by itself. Unit tests and continuous
integration can both be present while nothing is compared
with a recorded result.

The artifacts to inspect are a baseline test and the
continuous-integration record. The record should be a log
showing that the container was rebuilt from the recipe,
the analysis re-run, and its outputs compared with
recorded values within a stated tolerance. Absent that,
the honest reading of 'Level 4' is L2. Inspecting
`renv.lock` and the Dockerfile tells you the capture
artifacts exist; only the CI record tells you the capture
works.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

The colleague almost certainly meant the National
Academies sense: a second cohort, collecting its own data,
found a consistent result. That is *replication*, a
statement about the durability of the finding, and it is
the sense in which the word is ordinarily used in health
research.

The reviewer read it in an artifact-badging frame, where
the pair of words attaches to re-execution rather than to
new data. Under the current 2020 ACM vocabulary the two
conventions actually agree, so the current standard cannot
explain the request. The miscommunication traces to one of
two places. One is the
pre-2020 ACM badging, which attached the two words in the
opposite direction. The other is a field usage in which
'reproduce' names an independent study rather than a
re-run. A reviewer
carrying the sense of the words from an older document into
a current one is misled silently, with no error to warn
them.

The practical resolution is that the container request is a
category error given what the colleague did. A container
would let the reviewer re-execute the *original* analysis,
which is not what the colleague claimed and not what a
second cohort demonstrates. The colleague should answer by
naming the convention, stating that the second cohort
collected its own data, and offering the artifact that
actually matches the claim, which is the second cohort's
own analysis code.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

The demonstration is the worked example of @sec-crisis in
miniature.

```r
draw <- function(kind) {
  suppressWarnings({
    RNGkind(sample.kind = kind)
    set.seed(42)
    sample(1:10, 5)
  })
}
original <- RNGkind()
draw('Rounding')
draw('Rejection')
suppressWarnings(RNGkind(
  kind = original[1], normal.kind = original[2],
  sample.kind = original[3]
))
```

The two calls share a seed and return different draws.
Restoring the original generator afterward matters, since
`RNGkind()` sets session state that would otherwise persist
and silently affect everything downstream.

The layer demonstrated is the **session configuration**
layer, which sits above the package versions and below the
analysis code. It is the layer this chapter singles out as
only partially pinned at L2. An image fixes the locale and
the time zone, and the R version it carries fixes the
*default* sampler. However, the RNG kind, the contrasts,
and the number of printed digits are all settable from
inside the session and are not properties of the image.

A container alone would not protect against this because
the change is made by the analysis, inside the container,
after the environment is fixed. Two runs of the identical
image produce different draws if the code sets the sampler
differently, or if a mounted `.Rprofile` does. The
protection lies in an explicit declaration, which a
heavier container cannot supply. Concretely, set
`RNGkind()` in the analysis, record it alongside the
seed, and treat it as part of the analysis code rather
than part of the environment.
:::

## Exercise 8

The layer is the **R runtime** layer of this chapter's
determinant stack, not the package-versions layer above
it, and not the analysis code further up. The sampler
that turns a seed into a draw is, by default, a behavior
of R itself. The change arrived with a new R release
rather than with a new package version or an edited
script. Exercise 6 places the RNG kind in the session
configuration instead because there the analysis
*overrides* the default; here the default itself moved.

By this chapter's own stack figure, the R runtime is
secured only at **L2, pinned environment**, the same rung
that secures the operating system and system libraries.
A lockfile at L1 fixes the packages but not the R version
underneath them. So an L0 or L1 analysis in 2018 would
have had no protection at all. Whichever R release the
person re-running it happened to install would supply
whichever sampler that release shipped. Only an analysis
built from a container image pinned to an R release predating 3.6.0
would have run the old sampler regardless of when it was
restored. That protection is exactly what the L1-to-L2
step of this chapter's worked example buys, and what a
lockfile alone does not.
:::

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-levels}

| Rung or rule | What it means or checks |
|---|---|
| L0 locatable | Source under version control; nothing computational pinned |
| L1 pinned packages | A lockfile (`renv.lock`) records every package's exact version |
| L2 pinned environment | A container or Nix recipe also fixes the OS, R runtime, and system libraries |
| L3 verified | A baseline test compares regenerated outputs with recorded values, within a stated tolerance, after a clean rebuild |
| Capture vs. validation | Capture (a lockfile, a container) sets the level; validation (CI, a baseline test) only confirms it (habit 5) |
| Reproduced (this book) | Same code, same data, re-run; contrast replicated: a new study, new data |
| `zzc verify --full` | Reports L3 only if the image rebuilds, tests pass, and a `test-baseline*.R` file ran |
| Honest statement | Name the rung, the artifact, and what remains exposed; never claim 'fully reproducible' (motto) |

## Further reading

- @nas2019 is the National Academies consensus report that
  fixes the reproducible-versus-replicable terminology this
  book follows; read its opening chapter for the definitions
  and the reasoning behind them.
- @peng2011 introduces the reproducibility spectrum that our
  ladder consolidates, and argues for reproducibility as a
  minimum standard when full replication is impractical; the
  earlier @peng2009 applies the idea to epidemiology directly.
- @leek2015 makes the case that reproducibility is a floor and
  not a ceiling, and @patil2016 offers a statistical framing of
  the distinction between reproducing a computation and
  replicating a finding.
- @acm2020 documents the artifact-review badges whose
  'available', 'functional', 'reusable', and 'reproduced'
  ordering grades related but different things from our
  ladder; read it alongside @nas2019 to
  see how the 2020 revision aligns the two vocabularies.
- @turingway2022 crosses the reproducibility axis with a
  what-varies axis, same or different data against same or
  different analysis, and is the most accessible community
  handbook for a first-year student.
- For the determinant stack and the capture-versus-validation
  distinction as a framework applies them, @sandve2013 and
  @wilson2017 give the practices, the former stressing the
  recording of random-number seeds and exact versions that the
  ladder's session-configuration layer names.
